Package org.uma.evolver.example.training.constrained

Class AsyncNSGAIIOptimizingNSGAIIForProblemDASCMOP5

java.lang.Object
org.uma.evolver.example.training.constrained.AsyncNSGAIIOptimizingNSGAIIForProblemDASCMOP5
public class AsyncNSGAIIOptimizingNSGAIIForProblemDASCMOP5 extends Object
Runs the asynchronous NSGA-II as meta-optimizer to configure NSGA-II for DASCMOP5, a problem with constraints, through TrainingRunner.

The first reference example of tuning on a problem with constraints. The base level uses NSGAIIDoubleConstrained.yaml, the parameter space of NSGA-II plus its constraintHandling parameter, so the constraint-handling technique is tuned with the rest of the configuration. With its default configuration (cdp) and 20000 evaluations, NSGA-II finds feasible solutions in about 6 of 10 runs on DASCMOP5, and their ICMOP ranges from -0.41 to 0.09: there is room both to fail less often and to improve the quality.

The objectives of the meta-optimizer are ICMOP (ConstrainedMultiobjectiveIndicator, the indicator of Vodopija, Tušar and Filipič) and EP, as recommended in docs/concepts/evaluation.rst. Since the training problem has constraints, each objective is 6k + 2v + Q (ConstrainedIndicatorValue): k runs without feasible solutions, their mean scaled violation v, and the indicator on the feasible solutions, capped at its threshold (1 for both). With a single run per configuration, a configuration that finds feasible solutions has both objectives at most 1, and one that does not has them above 6.

The live plot of the meta-optimizer's front is on, to watch the search: the first configurations that fail appear above 6, and the front then moves below 1, where the configurations are compared by their quality.

The whole population of the meta-optimizer is written too (writePopulation), since the non-dominated configurations hide those without feasible solutions as soon as one has them. In the asynchronous NSGA-II every evaluated configuration enters the population while it has fewer than 50, so the checkpoint at evaluation 50 shows how many configurations of the random initial population fail; later, a configuration that fails competes to enter and is discarded at once, so the checkpoints show when the whole population becomes feasible, not every failure.
